687.title: Yom HaShoah
687.hook: Holocaust Remembrance Day, in spring: candles lit and names read aloud
687.howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, the twenty-seventh of Nisan, Israel stops for a two-minute siren, and communities around the world hold ceremonies with memorial candles, survivors' testimony, the reading of names, Kaddish and the memorial prayer El Malei Rachamim.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why the Omer mourns: Akiva's students. Your line was honor each other. Did you tell someone what you honor in them? Today, a newer day of mourning, inside the same weeks. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

On one spring morning each year, a siren sounds across Israel, and it holds for two minutes. On highways, cars stop in the middle of the lanes. Drivers open their doors and step out, and stand beside them, still. In offices, people rise from their desks. In shops, the cashier stops mid-sale. Children in schoolyards stand in rows. For those two minutes, much of the country stands still, and the only sound is the siren. Then it fades, and people get back in their cars. Elsewhere in the world, in synagogues, schools and community halls, the day is kept differently, but often with the same two things: candles, and names.
screen: `TEN IN THE MORNING.` → `CARS STOP ON THE HIGHWAY.` → `CANDLES, AND NAMES.`

segments.voice: Yom HaShoah is Holocaust Remembrance Day. Its full name in Israel is the Day of Remembrance of the Holocaust and the Heroism. Shoah is a biblical word for devastation, a storm that destroys, and it's become the Hebrew name for the murder of six million Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. Israel's parliament set the day in 1951, and wrote it into law later in that decade. It falls on the twenty-seventh of Nisan, less than a week after Passover ends. The date is tied to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which began on the eve of Passover, when Jews in the ghetto took up the few weapons they had against the German army. That's why the name includes heroism: remembering not only how people died, but how people resisted, in arms and in ordinary acts of keeping faith, keeping children alive, keeping names. The evening before, at Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem, survivors light six torches, for the six million. In many places, there's a ceremony of reading names, one after another, for hours. Its Hebrew name means: every person has a name. Not every community marks this date. Some Haredi communities remember the Holocaust on traditional fast days instead, such as Tisha B'Av or the Tenth of Tevet, partly because Nisan is a month the tradition keeps for joy. The ways differ. What they share is a refusal to let the numbers erase the people. Six million is a figure no one can picture. A name, read aloud, is a person.
screen: `SHOAH: DEVASTATION.` · `THE TWENTY-SEVENTH OF NISAN.` · `THE HOLOCAUST AND THE HEROISM.` · `EVERY PERSON HAS A NAME.` · then, large: `REMEMBER IN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle in silence. If you can, light one now, safely. If not, picture its flame. Don't say anything. Breathe slowly. If you know the name of someone who died in the Holocaust, from your family, your community, or a story you've read, hold that name in your mind. If you don't know one, hold the fact that each of the six million had one. Let the silence do the work. The bell holds the time.
Yom HaShoah. Holocaust Remembrance Day: candles, a siren, and names read aloud. Today's word.
Your line: remember in silence. Today, take two minutes, wherever you are, and stand or sit in silence for the names. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

screen: `DAY 687 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ISRAEL'S MEMORIAL AND INDEPENDENCE DAYS.`

688.title: Israel's memorial and independence days
688.hook: Yom HaZikaron honors the fallen, then Yom HaAtzmaut follows; communities worldwide mark them very differently, and some not at all
688.howItsDone: In Israel, Yom HaZikaron is marked with sirens and ceremonies at military cemeteries, and Yom HaAtzmaut begins at nightfall with a torch-lighting ceremony; Jewish communities elsewhere mark the days in many ways, some with added prayers such as Hallel, and some not at all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom HaShoah: candles, a siren and names. Your line was remember in silence. Did you find two minutes for it? A week later come two more days, side by side. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

A flag hangs at half-mast on a hill in Jerusalem. All day, families have stood at military cemeteries across Israel, by the graves of sons and daughters, brothers, parents. The radio has played only quiet songs. Then the sun goes down, and in a single ceremony the flag is raised to the top of the pole, torches are lit, and fireworks go up. Some of the same people who stood at the graves that morning will be at a barbecue the next afternoon. A day of grief, a day of joy, and one sunset between them. The calendar puts them back to back on purpose.
screen: `A FLAG AT HALF-MAST.` → `ONE SUNSET, THEN FIREWORKS.` → `BACK TO BACK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: The first day is Yom HaZikaron, the day of remembrance, on the fourth of the Hebrew month of Iyar. It honors Israel's fallen soldiers, and, in later years, civilians killed in attacks too. A siren sounds in the evening, and again the next morning. The second day is Yom HaAtzmaut, Independence Day, on the fifth of Iyar. It marks the declaration of the State of Israel in May 1948. When either day would touch Shabbat, the dates are moved. The move from one to the other is the point: the calendar ties them together, and the ceremony that closes the first day opens the second. Memory first, then celebration. Outside Israel, and within it, Jews mark these days very differently. Some communities hold memorial services and festive gatherings. Some add prayers; in religious Zionist synagogues, the psalms of praise called Hallel are often said on Independence Day. Some Reform and Conservative congregations have added readings for it. Haredi communities generally don't mark the days as religious occasions, and a few Haredi groups oppose the state on religious grounds. Some secular Israelis celebrate with no prayers at all, just flags and picnics. And for Palestinians, the same events of 1948 are remembered as the Nakba, the catastrophe. Today we're not asking which view is right. We're learning what's there: a pair of days, one of grief and one of joy, and a world of Jews who hold them in many different ways, and some who hold them not at all.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn how one community marks them. Before the bell, breathe, and think of a community you know, or could find out about: your own synagogue, a friend's family, a city in Israel, a community abroad. What might they do on these two days? Make a note to ask, or to read, today. Then sit with the shape of the days themselves: grief, a sunset, then joy. Think of a time in your own life when a loss and a celebration came close together. The bell holds the time.
Israel's memorial and independence days. Yom HaZikaron, then Yom HaAtzmaut: remembrance, then celebration, a sunset apart. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: memory before celebration. Today, before you celebrate anything, even something small, take a moment to remember what it cost someone. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: Jerusalem (Psalm 122)
689.hook: Yom Yerushalayim marks 1967 for many; everyone can pray "the peace of Jerusalem"
689.tomorrow: Shavuot: a wedding at the mountain
689.howItsDone: Psalm 122 is recited among the Songs of Ascents, often on Shabbat afternoons in winter; on Yom Yerushalayim, many religious Zionist communities add Hallel and festive prayers, while other communities do not mark the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Israel's memorial and independence days, a sunset apart. Your line was memory before celebration. Did you remember a cost before a joy? Today, one city, and one short psalm. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

Three times a day, in the standing prayer, Jews ask for Jerusalem to be rebuilt. At the end of every wedding, a glass is broken, and many say it's for Jerusalem. At the end of the Passover seder and of Yom Kippur, people say: next year in Jerusalem. For almost two thousand years, most Jews who said that had never seen the city, and never would. Then there's a short psalm, only nine verses, that pilgrims sang on their way up the hills to it. Its most famous line is a request that anyone, anywhere, can make.
screen: `THREE TIMES A DAY.` → `NEXT YEAR IN JERUSALEM.` → `A PILGRIM'S SONG.`

segments.voice: Psalm 122 is a Song of Ascents, one of fifteen psalms with that heading. Many scholars think pilgrims sang them on the way up to Jerusalem for the festivals. It begins with arrival. In the old Jewish translation: "I rejoiced when they said unto me: 'Let us go unto the house of the LORD.'" Then the pilgrims are standing inside the gates. And then the line people know: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem; may they prosper that love thee. Peace be within thy walls." Listen to the Hebrew: sha'alu shalom Yerushalayim. Shalom and Yerushalayim sound alike, and the psalm plays on it again and again. The rabbis noticed the city's name, too. A midrash says Abraham called the place Yireh, God will see, and Shem, Noah's son, called it Shalem, whole. So God, not wanting to offend either righteous man, joined the names: Yerushalayim. A city whose name holds seeing and wholeness. In modern times, Jerusalem has its own day. Yom Yerushalayim, on the twenty-eighth of Iyar, marks June 1967, when, during the Six-Day War, Israeli forces took the Old City and Jews could again pray at the Western Wall. For many, especially religious Zionists, it's a day of thanksgiving, with Hallel. Others don't mark it, or mark it with mixed feelings, because the city's future is still disputed. Jerusalem is holy to Christians and Muslims too, and home to all of them. That's why the psalm's line lasts. It doesn't ask who should hold the city. It asks for its peace.
screen: `A SONG OF ASCENTS.` · `LET US GO UNTO THE HOUSE.` · `SHALOM, YERUSHALAYIM.` · `YIREH AND SHALEM.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR JERUSALEM'S PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Psalm 122. If you can, find it now and read all nine verses slowly, out loud or under your breath. It takes less than a minute. If you can't, just repeat its middle line: pray for the peace of Jerusalem. Then sit with the city in your mind: its stones, its streets, the people of every faith who live there today. If you pray, this is a line you can pray. If you don't, simply wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
Jerusalem. Yerushalayim, the city of the Songs of Ascents, whose name the psalm plays on: shalom, peace. Today's word.
Your line: pray for jerusalem's peace. Today, when you hear news from Jerusalem, or from anywhere torn, say the psalm's line to yourself. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: Shavuot: a wedding at the mountain
690.hook: the rabbis picture Sinai as a wedding, the mountain held over the people like a canopy
690.howItsDone: On Shavuot, some Jews stay up through the night studying Torah, the Ten Commandments are read in the synagogue, and in some Sephardi communities a ketubah for Shavuot is read, portraying Sinai as the marriage of God and Israel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jerusalem and Psalm 122. Your line was pray for jerusalem's peace. Did the line come to you during the day? Today, the count of the Omer ends, and we arrive at the mountain. Day six hundred ninety.

At a Jewish wedding, the couple stands under a chuppah: a canopy, often just a prayer shawl or a cloth held up on four poles. A document is read, the ketubah, spelling out promises. Words are spoken. Something is given. And then a crowd that was holding its breath bursts into song. Now a second scene. A mountain covered in cloud and smoke, thunder, a horn growing louder and louder, a whole people gathered at its foot. On Shavuot, Jews celebrate that day at Sinai. And the rabbis said that what happened there was a wedding.
screen: `A CANOPY, A DOCUMENT, A PROMISE.` → `A MOUNTAIN IN SMOKE AND THUNDER.` → `WHAT IF IT WAS A WEDDING?`

segments.voice: Shavuot means weeks: the festival at the end of the seven weeks of counting. In the Torah it's a harvest feast, the first wheat. The rabbis tied it to the giving of the Torah at Sinai. And the wedding picture has old roots. The Mishnah, at the end of tractate Taanit, reads a verse from the Song of Songs about King Solomon's wedding day and says: that's the giving of the Torah. On that reading, God is the groom and Israel the bride. The Torah's own description of the day invites the comparison. In the old Jewish translation: "And Moses brought forth the people out of the camp to meet God; and they stood at the nether part of the mount." At the bottom of the mountain. But the Hebrew can also be read: underneath the mountain. The Talmud, in Shabbat 88a, takes that literally, and here the honest thing is to say the image isn't gentle. God, it says, held the mountain over them like an overturned barrel, and said: if you accept the Torah, good; if not, here will be your grave. The Talmud itself is uneasy, and adds that the people later accepted it fully, freely, in the days of Esther. Some later teachers took the same picture and softened it: the mountain overhead became the wedding canopy. And at the foot of it, the people's answer, which the Torah gives in the old Jewish translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken we will do." Some Sephardi communities read an actual marriage contract on Shavuot morning, a ketubah between God and Israel, a poem tradition credits to Israel Najara. A wedding at the mountain: a promise made under a canopy of cloud.
screen: `SHAVUOT: THE FEAST OF WEEKS.` · `THE DAY OF HIS WEDDING.` · `UNDER THE MOUNTAIN.` · `A KETUBAH FOR SHAVUOT.` · then, large: `A WEDDING AT THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread a promise you made. If you have one written down, wedding vows, a letter, a commitment you signed, an old journal entry, find it, and read it slowly. If not, remember one, word for word if you can. Breathe. Ask yourself, without judgment: how is this promise doing? What would it look like to make it again, freely, today? The bell holds the time.
Shavuot. Weeks: the festival at the end of the Omer, remembered as the day of Sinai, a wedding at the mountain. Today's word.
Your line: a wedding at the mountain. Today, renew one promise, out loud, to the person you made it to. Day six hundred ninety.

691.title: Shavuot: Ruth (Ruth 1:16)
691.hook: Ruth, the Moabite who chose to join: "whither thou goest, I will go"
691.howItsDone: On Shavuot, the book of Ruth is read in the synagogue, in some communities on the second day outside Israel; Ruth is honored as the model of a person who joins the Jewish people by choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot as a wedding at the mountain. Your line was a wedding at the mountain. Did you renew one promise? Today, the book read on Shavuot morning, about another promise. Day six hundred ninety-one.

Three widows stand on a road. The oldest, Naomi, is going home to Bethlehem after about ten years abroad, with nothing: her husband and both her sons have died. The two younger women are her daughters-in-law, both from the land of Moab. Naomi tells them, kindly and firmly: go back to your mothers' houses. You're young. Marry again. I have nothing left to give you. They weep. One of them, Orpah, kisses her mother-in-law goodbye and turns back, and the book doesn't blame her for it. The other, Ruth, holds on, and won't let go.
screen: `THREE WIDOWS ON A ROAD.` → `GO BACK, NAOMI SAYS.` → `ONE TURNS BACK. ONE HOLDS ON.`

segments.voice: What Ruth says next has been quoted at weddings, conversions and gravesides. In the old Jewish translation: "Entreat me not to leave thee," she begins, and then: "for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." She adds that only death will part them. Notice the order. People first, then God. Ruth chooses a person, then a people, then a faith, in that order. Jewish tradition came to see her as the model of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice. They arrive in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. Ruth gleans in the fields of a relative named Boaz, who treats her with care, and in the end they marry. Their son is Obed. Obed's son is Jesse. And Jesse's son, the book ends, is David, the king. So the great king of Israel had a great-grandmother from Moab, a foreigner who chose to stay. Why read it on Shavuot? Several reasons are given. The story happens during the harvest, from barley to wheat, and Shavuot is the wheat harvest festival. Ruth accepts the Torah freely, as Israel did at Sinai. And a tradition holds that David was born and died on Shavuot. A midrash adds one more: this little book, it says, has no laws of purity or impurity; it was written only to teach how great the reward is for those who do kindness. Chesed, loving-kindness, runs through every chapter: Ruth to Naomi, Boaz to Ruth, and Naomi, who in the end holds the baby close.
screen: `ENTREAT ME NOT TO LEAVE THEE.` · `PEOPLE FIRST, THEN GOD.` · `GREAT-GRANDMOTHER OF DAVID.` · `A BOOK OF KINDNESS.` · then, large: `WHITHER THOU GOEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome someone who chose you. Breathe, and think of someone who didn't have to be in your life, but chose to be: a friend who stayed through a hard year, an in-law, a stepparent, someone who joined your family or your community. Picture them on the road with you, holding on. Now think of how you'd let them know they belong. A word, a seat at your table, an invitation. Hold that for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Shavuot. The feast of weeks and of Sinai, when the book of Ruth is read: a woman who chose to join. Today's word.
Your line: whither thou goest. Today, tell the person you pictured, in your own words, that you're glad they came. Day six hundred ninety-one.

692.title: Shavuot: milk and greenery
692.hook: dairy meals, and greenery in homes and synagogues
692.howItsDone: On Shavuot it is a widespread custom to eat dairy meals, such as blintzes and cheesecake, and decorate homes and synagogues with greenery and flowers; some communities, following the Vilna Gaon, do not bring trees into the synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth on Shavuot, the Moabite who chose to stay. Your line was whither thou goest. Did you welcome someone who chose you? Today, what Shavuot puts on the table and on the walls. Day six hundred ninety-two.

Blintzes. Cheesecake. A noodle kugel heavy with cottage cheese. In some Sephardi kitchens, little pastries stuffed with cheese, or rice cooked in milk. A festival that remembers a desert mountain, thunder and the giving of the Torah, and the menu looks like a dairy aisle. Then look up. Branches over the doorways. Flowers on the table. In some synagogues, leafy boughs beside the ark, or roses wound around the reading table. The room smells like a garden. Nobody in the Torah's account of Sinai eats a blintz. So where did all this come from? Today: the milk and the green.
screen: `BLINTZES AND CHEESECAKE.` → `BRANCHES OVER THE DOOR.` → `WHERE DID THIS COME FROM?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Shavuot means weeks: seven weeks counted from Passover, and then this festival. The Torah gives it a harvest face, the feast of the first fruits of the wheat. The rabbis gave it a second face, the day the Torah was given. The Torah itself says nothing about cheese, and nobody can point to the day the custom started. What we have instead is a pile of explanations, offered side by side, and nobody has to choose one. One reaches for the Song of Songs, which speaks of honey and milk under the tongue; the rabbis read that as the Torah, sweet and nourishing. A second is practical. Once the laws of kosher food were given at Sinai, the story goes, nobody had properly prepared meat or pots ready, so they ate dairy. A third is a number game. Hebrew letters are numbers, and chalav, milk, adds up to forty, the days Moses spent on the mountain. A fourth is a pun, told with a smile. A psalm calls a mountain gavnunim, many-peaked, which sounds like gevinah, cheese. Now the green. A common explanation says that Sinai, a bare desert mountain, burst into bloom when the Torah was given. Some point to a detail in Exodus: the flocks were told not to graze in front of the mountain, so, they say, there must have been grass. Others connect it to a teaching in the Mishnah that on Shavuot the world is judged for the fruit of the trees. Not every community does it. Some, following the Vilna Gaon, leave trees out of the synagogue; others fill it with flowers. Put it together and Shavuot looks like a farm and tastes like a kitchen. A teaching that came down a mountain in fire is remembered with food that nourishes and leaves that grow.
screen: `SHAVUOT: SEVEN WEEKS.` · `MILK: SWEET AS TORAH, OR FORTY DAYS.` · `A DESERT MOUNTAIN IN BLOOM.` · `NOT EVERY COMMUNITY DOES IT.` · then, large: `GREEN AND MILK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring a green branch inside. A sprig from a tree, a leaf from the sidewalk, a stem of mint from the fridge, or just turn a houseplant so you can see it. Hold it, or set it in front of you. Look at the veins, the way the stem carries water out to the edges. Breathe slowly. Think of one thing you were given, a lesson, a habit, a sentence someone said, that kept growing in you long after it was handed over. Let your eyes rest on the green while you hold it in mind. The bell holds the time.
Shavuot. Weeks: the festival seven weeks after Passover, of first fruits and the Torah given, kept with dairy meals and greenery. Today's word.

Your line: green and milk. Today, eat one thing slowly, something green or something made with milk, and let it remind you that what we're given is meant to feed us and grow. Day six hundred ninety-two.

693.title: The Seventeenth of Tammuz
693.hook: a fast for the breach of Jerusalem's walls, beginning the Three Weeks
693.howItsDone: On the Seventeenth of Tammuz observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall, with a special Torah reading and added prayers; it begins the Three Weeks, when some communities hold no weddings and limit music until Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shavuot, with blintzes and branches. Your line was green and milk. Did something green come inside? Today the calendar turns, from harvest toward mourning. Day six hundred ninety-three.

Yom Kippur and the ninth of Av, the two long Jewish fasts, begin at sunset. This one begins at dawn. On a summer morning, while it's still dark, some people are up eating a quick breakfast and drinking as much water as they can. Then nothing, no food, no drink, until the stars come out. It's a long day at the height of summer. There's no special meal at the end, no famous melody, no crowd. Plenty of people walk past the date without noticing. But in the synagogue, the Torah is read and extra prayers are said, and a season has started. The day remembers a wall.
screen: `A FAST FROM DAWN.` → `A LONG SUMMER DAY.` → `IT REMEMBERS A WALL.`

segments.voice: Tammuz is a summer month in the Hebrew calendar, and on its seventeenth day the Mishnah gathers a run of disasters. It lists five. Moses broke the tablets, coming down the mountain to find the golden calf. The daily offering in the Temple stopped. The walls of Jerusalem were breached. A man called Apostomus burned a Torah scroll. And an idol was set up in the sanctuary. Some of these we can place; some we can't. Nobody is sure who Apostomus was. The walls bring a puzzle of their own. The book of Jeremiah says that when the Babylonians broke into Jerusalem, it was on the ninth of the month, not the seventeenth. The Talmud notices this, and answers that the seventeenth belongs to the second wall, when the Romans broke in centuries later. The Jerusalem Talmud offers another answer: in the chaos, people lost track of the date. Either way, the fast keeps the breach, and the reason is worth sitting with. A city doesn't fall the day its walls are breached. It falls weeks later. The breach is the day the danger gets inside, the first crack. So this fast opens a season. Three weeks from today is the ninth of Av, the day both Temples are remembered as destroyed. The weeks in between have a name from the book of Lamentations, bein hametzarim, between the narrow places. Customs vary: some communities hold no weddings in these weeks, play less music, and some people don't cut their hair. And there's a promise attached. The prophet Zechariah says the fast of the fourth month, which is this one, will one day become a time of joy and gladness. Even the mourning is kept with an eye on mending.
screen: `FIVE DISASTERS, ONE DATE.` · `WHICH WALL? THE ROMANS' BREACH.` · `THE CRACK COMES FIRST.` · `THREE WEEKS IN THE NARROW PLACES.` · then, large: `WALLS BREACHED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one crack that needs mending. Sit still and let your breathing slow. Then walk, in your mind, around the walls of your life: a friendship, your health, your work, your home, the way you speak to someone close. Don't fix anything yet. Just look for the place where something small has started to give: a message you keep not answering, a resentment that's grown a little, a habit slipping. When you find one, stay with it gently. Name it. That's all. Noticing early is the work. The bell holds the time.
The Seventeenth of Tammuz. A fast from dawn to dark for the breach of Jerusalem's walls, and the start of the Three Weeks. Today's word.
Your line: walls breached. Today, take one small step on the crack you found: a text, an apology, a repair, a doctor's appointment you've been putting off. Day six hundred ninety-three.
